sites.name: Lunch Counter
sites.capacity: Large — dozens of parties on summer weekends, spread across a broad bench; scores of pre-built rock windbreaks, though the best-sheltered ones fill first
sites.water: Snowmelt only, and seasonal. Running meltwater usually appears at the upper end of the bench through early and mid summer, but it is not dependable — in a thin snow year or by late season the bench can be dry, so carry a stove and fuel to melt snow.
sites.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — this camp is above the 7,000 ft threshold that triggers it between May 1 and Sept 30. Bought through recreation.gov, valid for a single climbing trip; carry it and leave a copy in the windshield. Parking at the South Climb trailhead needs a recreation pass, and the climbing pass parking stub satisfies that within Mt. Adams Wilderness in season. Outside that window or below 7,000 ft, a free self-issued wilderness permit is what applies. Human waste must be packed out in the supplied bags.
sites.notes: The standard high camp for the South Climb and effectively the only sheltered ground on the route, a wide rubble bench under Suksdorf Ridge about four miles and 3,700 ft above Cold Springs. Sources put it anywhere from roughly 9,200 to 9,400 ft because the bench is long and people camp at both ends rather than at one spot. The rock walls left by earlier parties are the whole reason to camp here — wind funnels across the bench and an unprotected tent takes a beating — so plan on repairing a wall rather than finding a perfect one. The summit ridge east of here forms the Yakama Nation boundary; the South Climb stays on Forest Service ground, but do not descend or traverse east off the standard line.

sites.name: Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead
sites.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites plus overflow in the parking area; fills on summer weekends
sites.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
sites.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.
sites.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.

sites.name: Morrison Creek Campground
sites.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites, several strung along the creek
sites.water: Morrison Creek runs beside the camp but is seasonal and can be low or dry by late summer; treat what you take and do not count on it in August or September.
sites.permit: No climbing pass needed at this elevation — it sits well below the 7,000 ft line. A free self-issued wilderness permit covers travel into Mt. Adams Wilderness from here, and a recreation pass applies at the trailheads above.
sites.notes: The fallback camp when the upper road defeats a vehicle or when Cold Springs is full, about three miles below the South Climb trailhead on the same road. The 2012 Cascade Creek fire burned through here, so shade is patchy and there is standing dead timber to consider when choosing a tent spot in wind. Camping here means driving or walking the last steep section to the trailhead in the morning, which costs about an hour but keeps the option open when the road is rough.

sites.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
sites.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards
sites.water: Generally reliable through summer. Meltwater streams from the Adams Glacier snout and small tarns feed the meadows, and Killen Creek runs lower on the approach; filter everything, and expect surface streams to shrink late in a dry season.
sites.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the Killen Creek trailhead. Note the elevation carefully — at about 6,900 ft this camp sits just under the 7,000 ft threshold, so the camp itself does not require a Cascade Volcano Pass, but any climbing above that line between May 1 and Sept 30 does, so a party heading for the Adams Glacier or North Ridge needs one. Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking. Camp on durable ground and well back from water — this is fragile subalpine meadow.
sites.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. Roughly four miles and 2,300 ft of gain, an easy carry compared with the Lunch Counter, and it puts you directly under the glacier's icefall. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.

sites.name: Adams Glacier moraine bivy
sites.capacity: Very small — a few flat gravel or snow platforms for one or two tents; you may have to build a platform
sites.water: Meltwater from the glacier snout and moraine pools during the day, freezing overnight; workable in warm conditions but not a certainty. Most parties melt snow here rather than depend on running water.
sites.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — above 7,000 ft, May 1 through Sept 30, single trip, from recreation.gov. Outside that window a free self-issued wilderness permit applies instead. Pack out all human waste.
sites.notes: Parties attacking the Adams Glacier sometimes move above High Camp onto the moraines below the icefall to shorten summit day, with usable ground reported roughly between 7,100 and 7,700 ft depending on which rib and how the moraine has changed. Exact spots shift year to year as the glacier retreats and the moraine slumps, so treat any elevation given for it as approximate and be prepared to camp lower. It is exposed, rockfall from the moraine walls is a real consideration in warm weather, and there is no shelter at all — the trade is a shorter and colder-snow start onto the glacier. Whether the extra carry beats simply starting early from High Camp is argued both ways.
